rv.q: It Hot is a delight from start to finish.
“It Hot,” which opened at the Shubert Theatre tonight, manages to speak to the moment with sizzle, polish and expert understanding of how to please a crowd.
What could have been a dated drag farce ends up as a show that many will like immensely — a musical filled with fun, energy and heart.

That’s a pretty high standard, after all, and in its staging (by Casey Nicholaw), its revamped plot (by Matthew López and Amber Ruffin) and especially its songs (by Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman), “Some Like It Hot” clears the bar handily.
You'll leave this show with a smile on your face, and why not?
Without it, there is no surprise, intellectually or emotionally, and that is the case here, even though that original film was full of shocks and wonders.
By the end of it, all I could think is, Well, this is most of the way to being an incredible musical.

Audiences looking for a sugary shot of old-fashioned Broadway hooch will probably find much to satisfy here, but for all the energy expended and the talent on display, “Some Like It Hot” eventually begins to pall, all but numbing us to its charms by the relentlessness of its insistence upon them.
And in this silly, woozy, pretty show, with its endless tap numbers, it doesn’t exactly fit.
However, even if you go in totally cold — “Who’s Jack Lemmon?” God forbid — the show still disappoints as a stand-alone piece of theater.
Whether you like it hot, cold, or even in the pot, nine days old, you’re probably going to like this show.
If you’re a sucker for fast-paced glamour executed in high style, this is the one for you.
It’s noisy, lavish, unforgettable entertainment—in Broadway’s inspired version of Technicolor!
Some Like It Hot is a sizzling example of everything that Broadway does best, and it is not to be missed.
I imagine you'll make your own connections while viewing what is sure to be Broadway's next huge hit.
It Hot has everything a Broadway musical should have: a superb cast, a great score, terrific choreography and the highest production values.

And yet here comes Some Like It Hot, blazing a three-alarm fire with charm and wit to remind us of the joys that beautiful people, electric performances, exciting choreography and foot-stomping, finger-snapping, neck-pulsing music can inspire.
It Hot finds new vigor in roaring, raucous musical comedy.
It Hot is a booze-soaked, boisterous good time from start to finish.

With the exception of the lively title song, Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman’s (“Hairspray”) big band-style score is derivative and serviceable at best. But taken on the whole, “Some Like It Hot” is more than worth celebrating.
By delivering its pointed messages with such virtuosity and sheer spunk, “Some Like It Hot” manages to burn more brightly than most musicals of its kind.
Screen-to-stage adaptations are always tricky endeavors, and this one scores points for not just tracing the source but turning up some fresh ideas of its own...No one leaves thirsty.
...Natasha Katz’s warm lighting create the perfect atmosphere for this joyfully ridiculous show. Despite its occasional lapses into preachiness, it’s a really Hot time.

Indeed, acceptance is the key to just sitting back in your seat and embracing all the great stuff onstage in “Some Like It Hot” -- even if this overstuffed show sometimes feels that it should have been renamed “Some Like A Lot.”
For the most part, Some Like It Hot succeeds in its aim of simply entertaining its audiences with those two most glorious words in the English language.
Whatever puzzles there are in story and character in the Broadway show are swept along by the wonderful dancing and music that keeps the show rattling along.
That’s correct, if not exactly thrilling theater.
Never has more been way too much.
Whether you leave feeling entertained or overwhelmed probably depends on how eager you are for a fun time.
The music by Marc Shaiman and lyrics by Scott Wittman and Shaiman are smart and enhance the story, not just dropped in for a pause.
It Hot roars and sizzles hilariously, with a zest and an appeal that just can’t be denied.
It Hot is a wildly entertaining farce from start to finish.
This is fresh, full of laughs and sentiment, is not vulgar and is pure fun and entertainment.
Well, you could have knocked me over with a feather because I will forgive the flaws of Some Like It Hot as a theatrical experience to embrace the overwhelming authenticity.
Its creators desire to not offend anybody is actually more offensive than they think, tiptoeing when they should land with both feet hard.

cn.t: Critics praise this energetic film-to-stage adaptation for its dazzling choreography and updated sensibilities, though some find the modernized gender politics heavy-handed. Most agree it's a crowd-pleasing throwback musical comedy.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Shubert Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well.
Shubert Theatre's own seating notes flag obstructed or distant views from the far side balcony/mezzanine — worth avoiding unless it's the only option.

vs.sum: The Shubert Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, though some seats may require leaning forward for a full view. The sound quality is generally consistent and clear. While legroom is limited in some areas, the theater's historic charm and central location add to its appeal. Facilities are average, with typical lines at restrooms and concessions.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No wheelchair-accessible restrooms (available across street).
